[p. 346] Sūrat al-Ḥujurāt

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who believe, do not put forward﴾. *Qaddamahu* and *aqdamahu* are both transmitted with the middle radical doubled, and with the hamza, from *qadamahu*, meaning "he went before him," as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿He will lead his people﴾ [Hud 11:98]. The object is omitted so that the prohibition covers everything that might be put forward in the heart, whether speech or action. It is also permissible that no object is intended, and that the prohibition is directed at the act of going forward itself, as in His saying: ﴿It is He who gives life and causes death﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:80]. Or it may be from *qaddama* in the sense of *taqaddama* ("to go forward"), like *wajjaha* in the sense of *tawajjaha* ("to turn toward"). From this comes *muqaddimat al-jaysh* ("the vanguard of the army"), which is the group that goes ahead of it. This reading is supported by the recitation of Ya'qub: *lā taqaddamū*, with one of the two *tā'*s of *tatqaddamū* removed.

﴿before Allah and His Messenger﴾. The literal sense of the expression "I sat before so-and-so" (*jalastu bayna yadayy fulān*) is that you sit between the two sides that are level with his right and left, close to him. The two sides are called "two hands" (*yadayn*) because they lie in line with the two hands, being near to them, by way of extension, just as a thing is named after something else when it is adjacent to it. In this expression there is a kind of figurative speech called *tamthīl* (figurative representation), and it carries a great benefit: it depicts the vileness and heinousness of going ahead on any matter without following the models of the Book and the Sunnah. It is also possible that it is treated like your saying, "Zayd pleased me and his good condition," meaning "The good condition of Zayd pleased me." Thus here the meaning is "before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The benefit of this style is to indicate the strength of the particular distinction. Since the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) held a station with Allah that is not hidden, the verse took this course. This also prepares the ground for what He censured them for: raising their voices above his voice (ﷺ). For whoever Allah has favored with this preference and singled out with this distinction, the least that is due to him is reverence and veneration, that voices be lowered in his presence.

It is related from al-Ḥasan that some people slaughtered on the day of al-Aḍḥā before the prayer, so this (verse) was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded them to repeat the slaughter with another sacrifice. It is also related from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that it was revealed concerning the prohibition of fasting on the day of doubt.

﴿And fear Allah﴾. For if you fear Him, fear will restrain you from the forbidden putting forward.

﴿Indeed Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of what you say,

﴿All-Knowing﴾ of what you do. And one such as Him deserves to be feared.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 49, verse 2:

﴿O you who have believed﴾. Repeating the address to them is a summons to renew their insight at every address that comes to them, and a prompt to them, so that they do not become heedless of their reflection.

﴿Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾. That is: when he speaks and you speak, you must not let your voices go beyond the level his voice reaches, and you must lower them, so that his speech is higher than yours and his loudness is conspicuous above yours, until his precedence over you is evident and his priority in your eyes is clear.

﴿And do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another﴾. That is: when you address him while he is silent, beware of deviating from what you have been forbidden, namely raising the voice. Rather, you must not reach with your speech the loudness that prevails among you, and in addressing him you must deliberately use gentle speech, close to a whisper, which is the opposite of loudness. Or do not say to him, "O Muhammad, O Ahmad," but address him with prophethood, dignity and honour. When this verse was revealed, Abu Bakr and Umar did not speak to the Prophet (ﷺ) except like one confiding in secret. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, who was hard of hearing, had a loud voice, and whenever he spoke he raised his voice, and sometimes he would speak to the Prophet (ﷺ) and hurt him with his voice. The *kaf* of comparison, *kaf al-tashbih*, is in the place of the accusative: that is, do not speak loudly to him with a loudness like the loudness of some of you to others. In this there is evidence that they were not forbidden from loudness absolutely, so that they could address him only in a low voice; rather they were forbidden from a specific loudness, namely the loudness described as resembling what they had become accustomed to among themselves, which is the absence of regard for the majesty of prophethood and the greatness of its station.

﴿Lest your deeds be rendered void﴾. It is in the accusative position, as an object of purpose, *maf'ul lahu*, linked to the meaning of the prohibition. The meaning is: "Refrain from what you have been forbidden, lest your deeds be voided," that is, out of fear of their being voided, with the omission of a noun (*al-mudaf*) being understood.

﴿while you do not perceive﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 49, verse 3:

﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah﴾. The subject of "inna" (indeed) is complete here. "In the presence of the Messenger of Allah": the meaning is that they lower their voices in his assembly, out of reverence for him.

﴿Those﴾ is the subject (mubtada') of a nominal sentence whose predicate (khabar) is: ﴿those whose hearts Allah has tested for piety﴾. The relative clause (silah) of "alladhina" (those who) is complete at his words "for piety". ﴿Those﴾ together with its predicate forms the predicate (khabar) of "inna". The meaning is: "He purified them for piety," from the expression "imtahana al-dhahab" and "fatanahu," when one melts gold, separating its pure essence from its impurities and cleansing it. Its real meaning is: "He treated them as one who tests, and found them sincere." It is reported from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that it means "He removed desires from them." And "al-imtihan" is an "ifti'al" form from "mahanahu," which signifies a thorough testing or a severe trial.

﴿For them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾. This is another sentence. It is said that it was revealed concerning the two Shaykhs, may Allah be pleased with both of them, because of what proceeded from them of lowering their voices. This verse, with the arrangement in which it is ordered, placing those who lower their voices as the subject of the emphasizing "inna," and making its predicate a sentence of a definite subject and a definite predicate together, the subject being the demonstrative pronoun, and the resumption of the sentence which contains what their recompense is for their deeds, and the presentation of the recompense indefinite with its matter left vague, indicates the utmost esteem and approval of the act of those who lower their voices. And in it there is an implicit rebuke of the great wrong committed by those who raise their voices.

(p-349) ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the private chambers, most of them do not use their reason﴾. It was revealed concerning the delegation of Banu Tamim. They came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at midday while he was sleeping. Among them were al-Aqra' ibn Habis and Uyayna ibn Hisn. They called out to the Prophet ﷺ from behind his chamber and said: "Come out to us, O Muhammad, for our praise is an adornment and our blame is a disgrace." So he awoke and came out.

"Al-wara'" (الْوَرَاءُ, "behind") is the direction that a person's shadow conceals from you, whether from behind or in front. "Min" (مِن) is used for ibtida' al-ghaya (indicating the starting point), meaning that the calling originated from that place.

"Al-hujra" (الْحُجْرَةُ) is a piece of land enclosed by a wall that surrounds it. It is of the pattern fu'lah in the sense of maf'ulah, like "al-qabdah" (a handful). Its plural is "al-hujurat" (الْحُجُرَاتُ) with two damma vowels, and "al-hujarat" (الْحُجَرَاتُ) with a fatha on the jim, which is the qira'ah (recitation variant) of Yazid. The intended meaning is the chambers of the wives of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, each of whom had a chamber, and their calling was from behind them. Perhaps they dispersed among the chambers searching for him, or they called out to him from behind the chamber in which he was, but the word was pluralised out of reverence for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

The verb, although it is attributed to all of them, may be carried out by some of them, while the rest were content with it, so it is as if they all carried it out. "Most of them do not use their reason": it is possible that among them were some who were excluded from this judgement, and it is possible that the intended meaning is a general negation, since paucity may be used in the sense of negation.

The manner in which this verse was revealed contains, as is clear, the following points of honour for the station of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Among them is the condemnation of those who shouted at him, as foolish and ignorant. Among them is the use of the word "al-hujurat" as a metonym for the place of his seclusion and his midday rest with some of his wives. Among them is the use of the definite article rather than an idafah (construct phrase).

If a reflective person considers from the beginning of the surah to the end of this verse, he will find it to be so. Consider how it began by making obligatory that matters relating to Allah and His Messenger be put ahead of all other matters, without restriction. Then it followed that prohibition with what belongs to the same category of advancing, namely raising the voice and speaking loudly, as if the first were a foundation for the second. Then it praised those who lower their voices, to show the great standing they have with Allah. Then it followed this with something more grave and more complete in its ugliness: shouting at the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in his private time from behind the walls, (p-350) as one shouts at the least important of people. This is to draw attention to the monstrousness of what they dared to do, because the one whom Allah has raised in rank above being addressed loudly, the conduct of these people was an evil that had reached a degree of extreme impropriety.

﴿And if they had been patient﴾, meaning: if their patience had held firm. The position (i'rab, grammatical case) of "أنَّهم صَبَرُوا" (annahum sabarū, "that they were patient") is in the nominative, as the agent (fa'il) of the verb. "Al-sabr" (patience) means restraining the self from being drawn after its desires. God the Exalted said: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 28]. The saying "ṣabara 'an kadha" ("he was patient regarding such-and-such") has its object omitted, and the omitted object is "the self (al-nafs)." It has been said: "Patience is bitter, and none swallows it but a free man." His words ﴿until you come out to them﴾ indicate that if he had come out, but his coming out had not been to them and for their sake, it would have been necessary for them to be patient until they knew that his coming out was to them, ﴿it would have been﴾, that patience, ﴿better for them﴾, in their religion. ﴿And God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, abundant in forgiveness and mercy, and vast in both, so He will not restrict His forgiveness and His mercy from these people if they repent and turn back to Him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 49, verse 6:

﴿O you who have believed, if there comes to you a deviator with information﴾. They agreed that it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn 'Uqba, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had sent as a collector (of zakat) to the Banu al-Mustaliq. There had been a enmity between him and them in the Jahiliyya. When he approached their dwellings, they rode out to meet him, and he assumed they were going to fight him, so he returned and said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "They have apostatized and withheld the zakat." So he (ﷺ) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid, who found them praying, and they handed over the charities to him, and he returned. The indefiniteness of "deviator" and "information" implies generality over deviators and reports, as if he had said: "Any deviator who comes to you with any information."

﴿so verify﴾: pause over it, seek to clarify the matter and uncover the truth, and do not rely on the word of the deviator, because whoever does not guard himself against the category of deviance does not guard himself against lying, which is a kind of it. The verse indicates the acceptance of the report of a single trustworthy (ʿadl) person, for if we were to suspend judgment regarding his report, we would equate him with the deviator, and the specification of him would be without benefit. "Al-fusuq" means going out from something. It is said: "The date-palm fruit came out (fasaqat) from its skin." From its inverted form: "I cracked (faqastu) the egg," meaning when you break it and take out what is in it, and also from its inverted form: "I qafastu the thing," meaning when you take it out of its owner's hand, usurping it from him. Then it was used for going out of moderation by committing major sins. Hamza and ʿAli read: "fatathabbatu" (so verify). "Al-tathabbut" and "al-tabayyun" are close in meaning; both mean seeking firmness, clarity and recognition.

﴿lest you harm a people﴾: lest you harm.

﴿in ignorance﴾: a circumstantial clause, meaning: ignorant of the reality of the matter and the essence of the story.

﴿and then become, over what you have done, regretful﴾: then you become, i.e., you turn into.

﴿Regret﴾ is a kind of grief, namely that you are distressed over what has befallen you, wishing it had not happened; it is a grief that accompanies a person as a lasting companion.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 49, verse 7:

﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah﴾. So do not lie, for Allah informs him, and the veil of the liar is then torn away. Or [it means]: return to him and seek his opinion. Then he said, resuming: ﴿If he were to obey you in much of the matter, you would surely be in distress﴾, meaning you would fall into hardship and ruin. This indicates that some of the believers had made it seem good to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to attack the Banu al-Mustaliq, and to accept the words of al-Walid, while others among them were restrained, and their earnestness in piety held them back from daring to do that. These are the ones He excepted by His saying: ﴿But Allah has made faith beloved to you﴾. It is also said: they are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety. Since the description of those to whom Allah made faith beloved differed from the description of those previously mentioned, the particle ﴿lakinna﴾ (but, "lakinna") was placed in its exact position of istidrak (correction), which is the opposition of what follows to what precedes, in negation and affirmation.

﴿And He has made it attractive in your hearts and made disbelief hateful to you﴾, and disbelief is the covering up of Allah's blessings and denying them through ingratitude.

﴿And defiance﴾ (fusuq), which is departing from the clear path of faith by committing major sins.

﴿And disobedience﴾ (ʿisyan), which is refusing to submit to what the Lawgiver has commanded.

﴿Those are the rightly guided﴾, i.e., those excepted are the rightly guided, meaning they reached the path of truth and did not deviate from uprightness. And "rushd" (rushd, right guidance) is steadfastness upon the path of truth together with firmness in it, from "al-rashadah," which is the rock.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 49, verse 8:

﴿As a bounty from Allah and a favour﴾. Al-fadl (bounty) and al-ni'mah (favour) carry the sense of al-ifdal (bestowing) and al-in'am (conferring benefits). They are in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: He made it beloved to you and made disbelief, wickedness and disobedience hateful to you, for the sake of bounty and favour.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of the states of the believers and of the distinctions and differences among them,

﴿All-Wise﴾, when He bestows bounty and confers favour through divine success upon the most excellent.

And if two groups of the believers fight, then make peace between them.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stopped at the gathering of some of the Ansar while he was riding a donkey. The donkey urinated, so Ibn Ubayy held his nose and said: "Let go of your donkey, for its stench has harmed us." Abdullah ibn Rawaha said: "By Allah, the urine of his donkey is more fragrant than your musk." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) moved on, and the dispute between them went on until they abused one another and came to blows. Their two peoples, the Aws and the Khazraj, came, and they fought with sticks, and it was said: with their hands, sandals and palm fronds. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned to them and reconciled them.

The verse was revealed about this. The verb "iqtatalu" (fight) is in the plural, taking account of the meaning, since the two groups are in the sense of "the people" and "the men." The dual "baynahuma" (between them) is used taking account of the wording.

Then if one of them transgresses against the other.

"Al-baghy" (transgression, rebellion): arrogance, injustice, and refusal to make peace.

So fight the one that transgresses until it returns to the command of Allah. "Tafi'" means "turns back," that is, returns. "Al-fay'" (return) is the term for returning, and it is also used for the shade and for spoils of war. The shade is called fay' because it returns after the sun has cancelled it out ("naskh al-shams"), and spoils (al-ghanima) are what returns from the wealth of the disbelievers to the Muslims. The ruling on a rebellious group is that it must be fought as long as it continues fighting; when it ceases and lays down its hands from battle, it is left alone.

To the command of Allah, which is mentioned in His Book: reconciliation and the removal of enmity.

If it returns, from transgression, to the command of Allah,

then make peace between them with justice, with equity.

And act justly. This is a command to practise "qist" (justice) in general, after having been commanded to do so in the reconciliation between them.

Indeed Allah loves those who act justly, that is, the just. "Al-qast" can mean injustice, and "al-qist" means justice. The verb derived from it is "aqsata," and its hamza (alif of "a-") indicates privation, meaning he removed "qast," which is injustice.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 49, verse 10:

﴿The believers are but brothers, so make reconciliation between your two brothers.﴾ This is an affirmation of what was imposed upon whoever takes charge of reconciling those among the believers between whom hostility has arisen, and a clarification that faith has tied together its adherents by a near cause and a close kinship, which, if it does not surpass brotherhood, does not fall short of it. Then custom has run that when something like this arises between two brothers by birth, the bystander is obligated to hasten to remove it and dispel it by reconciling the two. Brotherhood in religion is more deserving of this. "إخْوَتِكُمْ" (*ikhwatikum*, "your brothers"), "يَعْقُوبُ" (Ya'qub).

﴿And fear God, that you may receive mercy.﴾ That is: fear God, for taqwa (God-consciousness) will move you toward mutual connection and harmony, and when you do that, the arrival of God's mercy to you is hoped for. The verse indicates that rebellion (*baghy*) does not remove the name of faith, because He called them "believers" despite the presence of rebellion.

﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people; perhaps they may be better than them; and let not women ridicule [other] women; perhaps they may be better than them.﴾ "Al-qawm" (a people, a group) refers specifically to men, because they are the ones who manage the affairs of women. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 34]. In origin it is the plural of "qa'im" (standing), like "sawm" and "zawr" are plurals of "sa'im" (fasting) and "za'ir" (visiting). That al-qawm is restricted to men is clear in the verse, for if women were included in "qawm," it would not say "and [let not] women [ridicule women]." Zuhayr confirmed this in his saying:

؎ I do not know, and I do not think I shall know... whether the Al Hisn are a qawm or nisa'

As for the expression "qawm Fir'awn" (the people of Pharaoh) and "qawm 'Ad" (the people of 'Ad), where the males and females are both meant, the word qawm does not in fact encompass both groups; rather, the intention is to mention the males and omit mention of the females, because they follow their men.

The indefiniteness of "qawm" and "nisa'" allows two meanings: that it means "some of the believing men and women should not ridicule others among them," or that it intends generality (ishya'), so that every group among them is forbidden from mockery. The verse did not say "a man from a man" or "a woman from a woman" in the singular, to inform that more than one of their men, and more than one of their women, had undertaken mockery, and to express the gravity of the matter they were engaged in.

His saying ﴿perhaps they may be better than them﴾ is a resumed sentence (kalam mustani'af), coming as a response to one who asks about the reason for the prohibition. Otherwise, grammatically, it should have been connected to what precedes it with "fa" (so). The meaning is that each person must believe that the one being mocked may be better in the sight of Allah than the mocker, since people have knowledge only of outward appearances and do not know inner secrets, while what weighs in the sight of Allah is the purity of hearts. Therefore no one should dare to mock someone whom his eye looks down upon when he sees him in shabby condition, or with a physical defect, or not eloquent in conversation, for perhaps that person is more sincere in heart and more God-fearing than one who is the opposite of his description, and so he wrongs himself by belittling one whom Allah has honored. 

From Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): "Affliction is entrusted to speech. If I were to mock a dog, I would fear that I might be transformed into a dog."

﴿And do not defame one another﴾: do not stab at the people of your religion. "Al-lamz" means to stab and to strike with the tongue. "Wa la tulammizu" is read by Ya'qub and Sahl. The believers are like a single soul, so when a believer defames a believer, it is as if he defamed himself. It has also been said that its meaning is: "Do not do what you would be defamed for," because whoever does what deserves defamation has, in reality, defamed himself.

﴿And do not insult one another with nicknames﴾: "al-tanabuz bil-alqab" is calling one another by them. "Al-nabz" is a bad nickname. The forbidden nicknaming is that which the one so called dislikes, because it demeans him and disparages him. As for what he likes, there is no harm in it. It is narrated that a group of the Banu Tamim mocked Bilal, Khabbab, 'Ammar and Suhayb, and the verse was revealed. From 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her): that she used to mock Zaynab bint Khuzaymah, who was short. From Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): "The wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) reproached Umm Salamah for being short." It is also narrated that it was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays, who had a hearing impairment, so they used to make room for him in the gathering of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) so that he could hear. One day he came saying, "Make room," until he reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to a man, "Move over," but the man did not do so. He said, "Who is this?" The man said, "I am so-and-so." He said, "Rather, you are the son of such-and-such a woman," meaning a mother he had been reproached with in the Jahiliyyah. The man was embarrassed, and the verse was revealed. Thabit said, "I will never boast over anyone in lineage after this, ever."

﴿Wretched is the name of wickedness after faith﴾: "al-ism" here means "the mention," from their saying, "his name flew among people for generosity or for meanness." Its reality is what rose from his mention and was elevated among people. It is as if it were said: "Wretched is the elevated mention for the believers, by reason of committing these offences, that they be mentioned with wickedness." His saying "after faith" is a denunciation of combining faith with wickedness, which faith forbids, just as one says, "Wretched is the matter: after maturity, frivolity." It has also been said that among their insults to Jews who had embraced Islam was, "O Jew! O wicked one!" so they were forbidden from this, and it was said to them, "Wretched is the mention, that you mention a man with wickedness and Judaism after his faith."

﴿And whoever does not repent﴾ from what he was forbidden,

﴿then it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾: he used the singular and the plural for the word "man" (man), and [then gave regard to] its meaning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 49, verse 12:

﴿O you who have believed, avoid much of suspicion﴾. It is said: "jannabahu al-sharra" (جَنَّبَهُ الشَرَّ), meaning he kept him away from evil, and its real meaning is placing him at a side (janib). It takes two objects, as Allah (Exalted) says: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim: 35]. Its intransitive form is "ijtanaba al-sharra" (اِجْتَنَبَ الشَرَّ), which drops one object. What is commanded to be avoided is some suspicion, and that some is described as being much. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Indeed, some suspicion is sin﴾? Al-Zajjaj said: it is your suspicion of people of goodness that is bad. As for people of wickedness, we may suspect them of what has appeared from them. Or its meaning is: "avoid much of it" (اجْتِنابًا كَثِيرًا), or "guard against the much, so that guarding against the some takes place." "Al-ithm" (اَلْإثْمُ) is the sin that makes its doer deserving of punishment. From it comes the name for its punishment, "al-atham" (اَلْأثامُ), which is of the form "fa'al," like "al-nakal" and "al-adhab."

﴿And do not spy﴾, that is, do not pursue the faults (awrat) and defects of the Muslims. It is said: "tajassasa al-amr" (تَجَسَّسَ الأمْرَ), when he sought it out and searched for it. It is of the form "tafa''ul" from "al-jass" (touching/feeling out). From Mujahid: "Take what appears, and leave what Allah has concealed." Sahl said: "Do not search, seeking out the defects that Allah has concealed from His servants."

﴿And let not some of you backbite others﴾. "Al-ghiba" (اَلْغِيبَةُ) is mentioning someone with what is defective in his absence. It derives from "al-ightiyab," like "al-ghila" from "al-ightiyal." In a hadith: "It is that you mention your brother with what he dislikes. If it is in him, it is backbiting; if not, it is slander (buhtan)." From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Backbiting is the condiment of the dogs of people."

﴿Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his brother when he is dead?﴾ "Maytan" (مَيْتًا) is Madani. This is an image and depiction of what the backbiter takes from the honour of the one he backbites, in the most vile manner. It contains several intensifications: the interrogative, whose meaning is affirmation (taqrir); placing what is at the extreme of abhorrence in conjunction with love; attributing the verb to "ahadukum" (any of you), and the indication that none of the individuals would love that; that the image is not limited to eating human flesh, but the human is made a brother; and that it is not limited to the flesh of a brother, but he is made dead. From Qatada: "Just as you would hate it, if you found a rotting carcass, to eat from it, so hate the flesh of your brother while he is alive." "Maytan" is in the accusative as a state (hal) of the flesh or of "akhihi" (his brother). When he had established for them that none of them likes to eat the carcass of his brother, he followed that with His saying: ﴿So you have detested it﴾, that is, your aversion to it is established by soundness of intellect; so let it be established that you should detest what is its like of backbiting, by soundness of religion.

﴿And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance and Merciful﴾. "Al-tawwab" (اَلتَّوّابُ) is one who is emphatic in accepting repentance. The meaning: fear Allah by abandoning what you were commanded to avoid, and by regret over what has occurred from you of it. For if you fear Him, Allah will accept your repentance and bestow upon you the reward of the God-fearing who repent. It is narrated that Salman used to serve two men among the Companions and prepare their food. One day he slept and neglected his duty, so they sent him to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to seek some condiment for them. Usama was in charge of the food of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: "I have nothing." Salman informed them, and they said: "If we had sent him to the well of Sumayha, its water would have dried up." When they went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he said to them: "What is it that I see, the greenness of meat in your mouths?!" They said: "We have not eaten any meat." He said: "You have indeed backbitten, and whoever backbites a Muslim has eaten his flesh," then he recited the verse. It has also been said: "The backbiting of creation only arises from absence (ghayba) from the Truth."

﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female﴾, from Adam and Eve; or: each one of you is from a father and a mother. There is not one among you who does not descend in the same manner as the other, equal to equal, so there is no sense in boasting or preferring oneself in lineage.

﴿And We made you peoples (shu'ub) and tribes (qaba'il)﴾. "Sha'b" (people, the broadest grouping): the first of the six tiers (ṭabaqat) by which the Arabs were organized, namely: sha'b (people), qabila (tribe), 'imara (clan), batn (sub-clan), fakhdh (house), and fasila (branch). So the sha'b includes the qaba'il, the qabila includes the 'amA'ir, the 'imara includes the buṭun, the batn includes the afkhadh, and the fakhdh includes the fasa'il. Khuzayma is a sha'b; Kinana is a qabila; Quraysh is an 'imara; Quṣayy is a batn; Hashim is a fakhdh; and al-'Abbas is a fasila. It is called "shu'ub" because the tribes branched out from it.

﴿So that you may know one another﴾: that is, He arranged you into peoples and tribes so that some of you would know the lineage of others, and no one would be attributed to other than his fathers. It does not mean that you should boast of fathers and grandfathers, or claim superiority in lineages. Then He explained the quality by which a person surpasses others and gains honour and nobility before God, so He said: ﴿Indeed, the most honourable of you in the sight of God is the most righteous of you﴾.

In the hadith: "Whoever would be pleased to be the most honourable of people, let him fear God." And from Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both): "The nobility of this world is wealth, and the nobility of the Hereafter is piety."

It is also narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) circumambulated on the day of the Conquest of Mecca, praised God and extolled Him, then said: "Praise be to God, who has removed from you the arrogance and pride of the Jahiliyya. O people, people are of two kinds: a believing, pious person who is honourable before God, and a wicked, wretched person who is contemptible before God." Then he recited the verse.

And from Yazid ibn Shajara: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) passed through the market of Medina and saw a black slave saying: 'Whoever buys me, on condition that he does not prevent me from the five prayers behind the Messenger of God (ﷺ).' One of them bought him, then he fell ill, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) visited him, then he died, and [the Prophet] attended his burial. Some people said something about that." Thereupon this verse was revealed.

﴿Indeed God is All-Knowing﴾, of the nobility of hearts and their piety,

﴿All-Aware﴾, of the aspirations of souls in their desires.

The Bedouins say, "We have believed." (﴿قالَتِ الأعْرابُ﴾) That is, some of the Bedouins, because among the Bedouins are those who believe in God and the Last Day, namely the Bedouins of Banu Asad. They came to Medina in a year of drought, and they professed the testimony of faith, seeking charity and claiming a favour upon him.

﴿آمَنّا﴾ That is: outwardly and inwardly.

﴿قُلْ﴾ Say to them, O Muhammad,

﴿لَمْ تُؤْمِنُوا﴾ "You have not believed": you have not affirmed with your hearts.

﴿وَلَكِنْ قُولُوا أسْلَمْنا﴾ "But say, 'We have submitted.'" Faith (al-iman) is affirmation (al-tasdiq), and submission (al-islam) is entering into peace (al-silm) and leaving the state of being at war with the believers, by uttering the two testimonies. Do you not see His saying: ﴿وَلَمّا يَدْخُلِ الإيمانُ في قُلُوبِكُمْ﴾ "and faith has not yet entered your hearts"? So He informed that what comes from verbal affirmation without the heart agreeing with it is submission (islam), while what the heart agrees with the tongue about is faith (iman). This is in terms of the lexical meaning. As for the sharia, faith and submission are one, as is known. In "lamma" (not yet) there is the sense of expectation, and it indicates that some of these people will believe later. The verse also refutes the doctrine of the Karramiyya, who hold that faith is not in the heart but only in the tongue.

If you say: the structure of the sentence would require that it be said, "Say: do not say 'we have believed', but say 'we have submitted'," or "Say: you have not believed, but you have submitted." I say: this arrangement conveyed first the refutation of their claim, so it was said, "Say: you have not believed," with good manners, and He did not say explicitly, "You have lied." He placed "you have not believed," which is the negation of what they claimed to affirm, in its place, and He dispensed with saying "do not say 'we have believed'" because it would be offensive to address them with a phrase whose import is a prohibition on speaking of faith. He did not say "but you have submitted," so that it would be understood as a claim and an assertion, as their saying "we have believed" was. Had it been said "but you have submitted," it would have amounted to an acceptance and a validation of their words, and they are not validated. His saying "and faith has not yet entered your hearts" is not a repetition of the meaning of "you have not believed," since the purpose of "you have not believed" is the refutation of their claim, while His saying "and faith has not yet entered your hearts" is a specification of the time for what they were commanded to say. As if it were said to them: "But say 'we have submitted' at a time when the agreement of your hearts with your tongues has not been established," because this is a clause standing in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) relative to the pronoun in "qulu" (say).

﴿وَإنْ تُطِيعُوا اللهَ ورَسُولَهُ﴾ In secret, by abandoning hypocrisy,

﴿لا يَلِتْكُمْ﴾ "la yalitkum" (will not deprive you), "basri" (a reading of Basra),

﴿مِن أعْمالِكم شَيْئًا﴾ That is: He will not diminish for you any of the reward of your good deeds in the least. "Alata, ya'litu," "alat, yalit," and "lat, yalit" have the same meaning, which is diminishing.

﴿إنَّ اللهَ غَفُورٌ﴾ He covers up sins,

﴿رَحِيمٌ﴾ and is merciful in guiding them to repentance from their faults.

(p-359) He described the sincere believers, saying: ﴿The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger, then did not doubt﴾. "Irtaaba" (ارتاب) is the reflexive form (muṭāwaʿ) of "rāba-hu" (رابه), meaning when something causes him to fall into doubt accompanied by suspicion. The meaning is that they believed, and then no doubt entered their souls regarding what they believed in, nor any accusation against those whom they affirmed as truthful. Since certainty and the removal of doubt are the foundation (milāk) of faith, this was singled out for mention after the mention of faith, as an alert to its position, and it was joined to faith by the word "then" (thumma), which denotes delay, to indicate that it remains firm across distant, extended times, fresh and new.

﴿And strive with their wealth and their selves in the way of Allah﴾. It is possible that the object of striving is implied, namely the enemy who wages war, or Satan, or whim (al-hawa). It is also possible that "jāhada" is an intensification of "jahada" (to exert effort). It is possible that striving with the self is meant as fighting (al-ghazw), and that it encompasses all acts of worship together. Striving with wealth is like the deed of ʿUthmān in the army of hardship (jaysh al-ʿusra), and it may encompass zakat and everything related to wealth from acts of righteousness.

The predicate of the subject, which is "al-muʾminūn," is: ﴿Those are the truthful ones﴾, meaning those who were truthful in their saying "We have believed" and did not lie as the Bedouins of the Banu Asad lied; or they are those whose faith is a faith of truthfulness and reality. His saying "alladhīna āmanū" is a qualifier (ṣifah) for them. When this verse was revealed, they came and swore that they were sincere, so there was revealed:

"Say: Will you inform Allah of your religion?" That is: will you tell Him of the affirmation of your hearts?

"And Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, and Allah is Knowing of all things," [including] hypocrisy, sincerity, and other than that.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 49, verse 17:

﴿They consider it a favour to you that﴾ i.e., in that,

﴿they have submitted [literally: embraced Islam]﴾, meaning: by their Islam. And "al-mann" (the reminding of benefits conferred): it is the mentioning of favours, as an allusion to thanks, and we were forbidden from it.

﴿Say: Do not consider your Islam a favour to me; rather, Allah confers a favour upon you﴾, i.e., the favour belongs to Allah over you,

﴿that He guided you to the faith, if you are truthful﴾, that He guided you [to it], or because [He guided you] to the faith. [The condition means:] if your claim is valid and your assertion is true, but you claim what Allah knows to be otherwise. The answer to the conditional is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, and its estimated form is: "If you are truthful in your claim of faith in Allah, then the favour is Allah's upon you." And it was read: "in guiding you" [إن هداكم in place of أن هداكم].

Indeed, Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is Seeing of what you do.

With the ya' (reading "yaʿmalūn" with ي), it is the reading of Ibn Kathir (Makki), and this is a clarification that they were not truthful in their claim. That is, He (Exalted is He) knows every hidden thing in the world, and sees every deed you do, in your secret and your open conduct; nothing of it is concealed from Him. So how could what is in your hearts be concealed from Him?!
